Why Does it Matter for Decision-Making?
Managers often face too much customer feedback to read manually.
Sentiment analysis helps to answer:

Are customers mostly satisfied or dissatisfied?
Which problems are repeated most often?
Which operational area should management prioritize?

Interpretation
The analysis moves from general sentiment to concrete business problems.
Examples:

Customer service issue -> support and service recovery
Late flight -> punctuality and delay communication
Lost luggage -> baggage tracking and recovery
Cancelled flight -> rebooking and compensation

title: Decision Making with Sentiment Analysis in R
text:
Different Sentiment Analysis Methods








Method
Basic idea
Why not used / selected?




Lexicon-based
Uses predefined sentiment dictionaries
Selected because it is transparent and easy to reproduce in RStudio


Machine learning
Trains a model on labeled text data
Requires training/testing setup


Transformer-based
Uses context-aware models such as BERT
More complex for a short live demo


Hybrid
Combines dictionaries and machine learning
More advanced setup



In this project, I use a lexicon-based approach because it is transparent, reproducible, and suitable for a short RStudio demonstration.

title: Decision Making with Sentiment Analysis in R
text:
10.1 Main Negative Reasons
The following plot visualizes the most frequent reasons behind negative airline tweets. This is important for decision-making because each reason represents a possible operational problem.

negative_reasons |>
  slice_max(n, n = 8) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = reorder(negativereason, n), y = n)) +
  geom_col() +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    title = "Main reasons behind negative airline tweets",
    x = "Negative reason",
    y = "Number of tweets"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

title: Decision Making with Sentiment Analysis in R
text:
10.2 Frequent Sentiment Words
After tokenizing the tweets and matching the words with the Bing sentiment lexicon, the following plot shows the most frequent positive and negative sentiment words. This helps make the lexicon-based sentiment analysis more interpretable.

top_sentiment_words |>
  mutate(word = reorder(word, n)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = word, y = n, fill = sentiment)) +
  geom_col(show.legend = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(~ sentiment, scales = "free") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    title = "Most frequent positive and negative sentiment words",
    x = "Word",
    y = "Frequency"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

title: Decision Making with Sentiment Analysis in R
text:
10.3 Sentiment Score by Airline
The following plot provides an additional lexicon-based comparison across airlines. For each airline, the number of positive and negative sentiment words is counted. The score is calculated as positive words minus negative words, standardized per 100 sentiment words.

ggplot(
  lexicon_airline_sentiment,
  aes(
    x = reorder(airline, lexicon_score_per_100_words),
    y = lexicon_score_per_100_words
  )
) +
  geom_col() +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    title = "Lexicon-based sentiment score by airline",
    x = "Airline",
    y = "Sentiment score per 100 words"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()








These figures are used as supporting evidence. The final decision-making step still requires managerial interpretation, because lexicon-based sentiment analysis can miss sarcasm, context, or ambiguous meanings.
